newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends up, makes new post-Gulf War high.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends up, makes new post-Gulf War high.

text.p: NYMEX crude ended near its new post-Gulf War high hit late session Wednesday, reversing declines after heating oil's losses from bearish weather forecasts failed to trounce bullish oil fundamentals overall, traders said.
"The underlying fundamentals are too strong," said Bob MacMinn, president of petroleum consulting firm MPAS in Toronto.
January crude ended up 45 cents a barrel at $26.16, after breaking the post-Gulf War high of $26.10 to rise to a new high of $26.20 minutes before the market's close at 1510 EST.

"There is zero tolerance for error in the supply/demand balance. Heating oil inventories are low, but demand has been high, and it's not even winter yet," said MacMinn. He said refiners have met distillate demand through high production.
Traders also noted prompt crude recovered when it held technical support around $25.00 in the afternoon after being sent lower in the morning following an initial attempt to break $26.10 and failing.
January heating oil finished up 0.64 cent a gallon at 74.18 cents. January gasoline settled up 1.40 cents at 71.17 cents a gallon after hitting a contract high of 71.50 intraday.
Heat fell as low as 72.20 cents after cold weather expected in the U.S. Northeast was forecast to be not as drastic as first thought.

Weather Services Corp said an artic air mass which has pushed temperatures down 20 degrees below normal in some parts of the Midwest will moderate in the Northeast where temperatures will be at most eight degrees below normal by Saturday. The U.S. Northeast is the largest heating oil market in the world.
The National Weather Service said in its six to 10 day forecast that temperatures would average about normal in most of the Northeast.
Meanwhile, the American Petroleum Institute (API) said on Tuesday that distillate stocks, which are comprised of heating oil and diesel, grew one million barrels for the week ended December 13.

Refiner distillate production was a near record 3.6 million barrels a day, replenishing inventories which were now nearly at 94 percent of last year's level compared to a deficit in recent months of 20 percent.

"First I thought this was going to be a typical API market fade. Starting strong and then weakening," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown in New York. The API data was supportive for crude and gasoline in that it reported significant weekly draws in those stocks.
Traders said crude's January contract expiration on Thursday will force the market to decide whether it wants crude to continue above $26.00 in the back months.
"Tomorrow could be one of the most significant trading sessions all year," a dealer said.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
